To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
Workplace interventions to reduce smoking should be multi-faceted, with elements to meet the needs of employees at different points in the process of quitting.
employees want workplace smoking interventions to be voluntary, flexible, and to offer a range of different options to suit the different stages of readiness for change that employees are in.

employees who are not yet ready to change their behaviour need a range of different types of support to help them to change, whereas those who are already committed to change have a different set of needs and require a different range of interventions.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the question: “What do employees want from smoking cessation interventions?”
the views of smokers and non-smokers on smoking cessation interventions in the workplace.
the development of a conceptual model that can be used to inform the design of effective workplace interventions to reduce smoking.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
a multi-facetal workplace smoking intervention, which includes both voluntary programmes and restrictions or bans, can be effective in reducing smoking rates among employees.

“Workplace smoking cessation programmes should be multi-faceted, and should provide a range of support options to employees, to ensure the needs of all employees, at all stages of the smoking cessation process, are met.”
a multi-facetal workplace intervention that provides a range of support options for employees at different stages of readiness for behaviour change is likely to be most successful.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
a workplace intervention should be tailored to the needs and preferences of the employee and that the intervention should be multi-faceted.
the synthesis suggests that workplace smoking interventions should be multi-faceted and should be tailored to the employee’s readiness for change.
workplace smoking interventions are most likely to be effective if they are tailored to the needs of individual employees.
The main takeaway from our work is that
interventions that are designed to be effective for everyone will be ineffective for anyone.
workplace smoking cessation interventions should include elements to address all stages of change.
the workplace can be a very effective environment for smoking cessation interventions, provided that they are well-designed and implemented.
